Option 1: "جهد آن کن تا مگر نامت بماند جاودانی - جاودان کس را نشان باقی نخواهد ماند هرگز"  
The first line seems to encourage effort ("جهد آن کن") to make one's name eternal. The second line says that the name of the eternal one will never remain. Wait, that's a bit confusing. Maybe it's saying that even if you strive to make your name immortal, the truly eternal (جاودان) person's name won't stay. So perhaps it's about the futility of seeking immortality through one's name, or maybe contrasting mortal efforts with the eternal's unchanging nature.

Option 2: "فردا غبار کالبدش در هوا رود - دامن کشان که می رود امروز بر زمین"  
This talks about the body's dust being scattered in the air tomorrow, and the one who is dragging their skirt (maybe a metaphor for someone important or a ruler?) today on the ground. It seems to be about the transience of life and the impermanence of worldly status or power. The body turns to dust, and even those who are powerful now will leave nothing behind.

Option 3: "وانکه دردیش نباشد به جهان هیچ کس است - هیچ کس نیست که او را به جهان دردی نیست"  
The first line says "If there is no pain in the world for anyone, then there is no one in the world who causes pain for him." The second line is a bit tricky. It might be saying "There is no one who causes pain for him in the world that has no pain." So this is a bit paradoxical or philosophical. It's talking about the absence of pain and how if the world has no pain, then the person who is painless is not harmed by anyone. Maybe it's about the idea that if you're free from suffering, the world's suffering doesn't affect you.

Option 4: "هر چیز که شاید و نشاید برود - رفتند و رویم و هر که آید برود"  
This one is about everything that might or might not go away. The second line says "They have gone and returned, and whoever comes will go." So it's emphasizing the transient nature of all things—people come and go, everything is temporary.

Now, let's see the themes. Options 2, 3, and 4 all seem to deal with the impermanence of life, the transient nature of existence, and the inevitability of change. Option 2 talks about the body turning to dust and the present's fleeting nature. Option 3 is about the absence of pain and how that relates to the world's pain. Option 4 is about everything being temporary, coming and going.

Option 1, however, is a bit different. The first line encourages striving to make one's name eternal, but the second line says that the eternal one's name won't remain. This could be a paradox, suggesting that even if you try to achieve immortality, the truly eternal (maybe God or a divine figure) doesn't have a lasting name. But the main theme here seems to be the futility of seeking immortality through one's name versus the eternal's own name. The other options are about the transient nature of the physical or worldly things. Option 1 is more about the concept of immortality and the idea that human efforts can't achieve it, perhaps contrasting with divine eternity. 

Wait, but maybe I'm misinterpreting. Let me check again. Option 1's second line says "جاودان کس را نشان باقی نخواهد ماند هرگز." So "The sign of the eternal person will never remain." So if you try to make your name eternal, but the truly eternal one's name won't remain. That's a bit confusing. Maybe it's saying that the name of the eternal (like God) doesn't need to be shown, or that even if you strive for it, the eternal's name doesn't stay. It's a bit abstract, but perhaps the theme is that human attempts at immortality are in vain, while the eternal (divine) is beyond such things. 

Comparing with the others: Options 2, 3, 4 all emphasize the temporary nature of things—dust, pain, and the coming and going of people. Option 1 is more about the contrast between human striving for immortality and the eternal's own nature. So the deviation here is Option 1 because it's not just about transience but about the futility of seeking eternal recognition versus the divine's unchanging state. The others are more about the world's impermanence, while Option 1 has a different angle on immortality and divine vs. human.
